title: KV staging buffer bucketing and burst-soak headroom allocator
creator: Anika Rao
description:
Problem statement: production serving faces intermittent microbursts that overflow KV cache allocations for mixed-priority tenants. Current eviction-first strategies cause high tail latency for interactive requests and noisy downstream fallbacks. We need a lightweight allocator that carves a small, elastic 'staging buffer' for incoming KV insertions, applies time-based soak and bucket policies, and exposes a headroom band that prevents sudden eviction storms while preserving weight and activation footprints.

Goal: design and implement a staging-buffer-based headroom allocator that: (1) absorbs short bursts without immediate global eviction; (2) buckets staging allocations by tenant priority and request type; (3) enforces a probabilistic decay/soak so hot KV can survive expected short bursts but still be reclaimable; (4) integrates with continuous batching so the runtime can opportunistically commit or roll back staging entries at safe checkpoints; (5) provides telemetry and rollout knobs for safe canarying.

Scope: prototype allocator in runtime v1.23, simulator-driven validation, unit + integration tests on small clusters, and gradual canary rollout behind a runtime feature flag. Not in scope: wholesale redesign of weight layout or persistent-on-disk cache storage.

Design summary: we introduce three concepts: 1) staging buffer: a ring of ephemeral KV slots allocated per-GPU and per-tenant as a transient sink for newly activated KV entries; 2) buckets: each staging buffer is partitioned into N buckets (priority, model-size, request-class) with configurable quotas and overflow policies; 3) burst-soak policy: entries in staging are allowed a soak window (ms to seconds, configurable per-bucket). If entry survives soak, it may be promoted to main KV cache; if not, it is discarded. Promotion is coordinated with continuous-batching checkpoints so we avoid partial KV references across shards.

Memory model: the allocator treats GPU memory as three logical domains with explicit accounting strings for telemetry: weights (static), activations (ephemeral), and KV (split into main + staging). Headroom band is computed per-GPU as a percentage of total free memory plus a soft reserve for ongoing activations. The staging buffer consumes the headroom band and is reclaimable synchronously if memory pressure exceeds an emergency threshold.

Metrics and telemetry: new metrics to add: staging_alloc_bytes, staging_promote_count, staging_evict_count, bucket_pressure_ratio, soak_survival_ratio, per-tenant_staging_usage, staging_eviction_latency_ms, staging_spill_events. We will add tracing hooks to correlate staging events with request IDs and batching windows.

Rollout plan: implement behind feature flag 'staging_buffer_v1'. Start in internal test clusters -> 1% canary in SaaS cluster -> 10% -> 50% -> full. Canary checks: no increase in p95/p99 tail latency, staging_eviction_rate < 5% of insertions after soak, no increase in OOM events.

Acceptance criteria: see acceptance_criteria field.

Docs and artifacts: links below include design doc, simulator notebooks, and PRs.
acceptance_criteria: Simulator confirms >40% reduction in immediate eviction rate during synthetic microbursts (1-5s) while keeping average KV residency change within 10%
No regressions in p99 token latency (<= 5% relative change) on canary cluster after 2 days
Feature flag fully controllable per-deployment and per-GPU group
All new telemetry emitted at DEBUG and INFO level and documented
Unit tests cover soak logic and bucket overflow strategies; integration tests exercise continuous-batching checkpoint interaction
benchmarks: Local sim: mixed-tenant 50/50 interactive/batch with 10% microbursts: immediate eviction rate down 46% over baseline
Staging soak tuned to 800ms reduces p99 tail for interactive by 12% in microburst scenarios
Memory overhead: staging consumes <3% of total GPU RAM when within normal headroom allocations
updates: 2026-02-12: Kickoff meeting. Agreed on three-bucket prototype (high/medium/low priority) and soak windows initial defaults: 200ms/800ms/2s.
2026-02-20: Simulator prototype implemented by @Luca. Initial soak survival ratio inconsistent for batch-heavy tenants. Decided to add batch-discount factor to bucket quotas.
2026-02-27: Design review with PM and SRE. Action: add emergency synchronous reclaim path and per-tenant throttles to avoid cross-tenant OOM cascades.

2026-03-05: Integration demo in staging. Observed unexpected promotion races when continuous-batching checkpoint aligned with eviction. Plan: add lightweight checkpoint lock and commit/rollback markers to staging slots.
2026-03-12: Spike PR submitted for staging buffer allocator core. Added telemetry hooks and feature flag scaffolding. Next: tests and canary plan.
2026-03-12: Assigned rollout owner for canary monitoring: @Maya Chen.
tests: Unit: soak expiry/renewal, bucket quota enforcement, promotion logic under race conditions
Integration: run continuous-batching flows with simulated microbursts across 3-node cluster and validate no stale KV references after commit/rollback
Chaos: force an extra allocation spike while staging is enabled to validate synchronous reclaim path and ensure no OOMs
Performance: measure p50/p95/p99 token latencies with and without staging under representative workloads
risks: Promotion races with batching checkpoints can create partial KV references across GPUs; mitigated by commit/rollback markers and short-lived locks
Over-provisioning staging band could mask memory leaks if telemetry is ignored; require automated alerts when staging fraction grows > 15% sustained
Per-tenant fairness: naive bucket quotas could cause starvation for low-priority tenants during repeated microbursts
Operational complexity: added knobs may create operator confusion; include sane defaults and one-click disable
